strengths: Clear and timely contribution: the paper targets the polar decomposition/matrix sign subroutine in Muon, an increasingly relevant optimizer for LLM training, and identifies a real mismatch between classical high-precision numerical linear algebra methods and GPU-friendly low-precision deep learning needs.

The main technical idea is well motivated and elegant: adaptive minimax odd polynomial updates give a principled alternative to heuristic Newton-Schulz coefficient tuning, while preserving implementation simplicity through matrix-matrix products only.

The theoretical development is a significant strength. The paper proves a greedy optimality result for compositions of bounded-degree odd polynomials under a spectral-norm worst-case objective, connects the method to equioscillation/Remez approximation, and establishes super-exponential convergence.

The method is practical: the authors provide explicit degree-5 coefficients, discuss bfloat16 stability issues, and describe simple implementation details that make the method usable as a drop-in Muon replacement.

Empirical results are promising. Polar Express improves convergence on synthetic matrices and GPT-2 gradient matrices, and yields consistently better validation loss than Jordan and You coefficient choices in GPT-2 Small/Large FineWeb1B training sweeps.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is narrower than the claims suggest. The main training evidence is limited to GPT-2-style models on FineWeb1B, with no evidence on other architectures, token budgets, modalities, or larger modern LLM training regimes where Muon is most compelling.

The reported training gains are promising but not statistically characterized. The paper appears to report single runs per learning rate without seeds, variance estimates, or significance analysis, which makes it difficult to assess robustness given the modest absolute loss improvements.

The comparison set for end-to-end training is limited to recent polynomial Muon variants. The paper explains why rational/SVD/QR methods are unsuitable, but more direct runtime and quality comparisons, including optimized Newton-Schulz variants and Chen-Chow-style scaling in the actual Muon setting, would strengthen the empirical case.

The method depends on guessed lower singular-value bounds and finite-precision stabilizing heuristics. Although the paper discusses robustness, the practical sensitivity of the recommended coefficients across many real training matrices is not fully explored.

Some presentation and reporting issues reduce confidence: Figure 7's caption appears to reuse GPT-Small/AdamW numbers despite describing GPT-2-Large, and there are minor textual/typographical errors. These are fixable but noticeable in an otherwise technical paper.

Reproducibility is only partially supported in the manuscript. The paper gives code snippets and says a repository exists, but the reviewable artifact does not clearly specify all hyperparameters, seeds, exact implementation details, and logging needed to reproduce the LLM training results.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and concrete subproblem in modern LLM optimization: fast low-precision computation of the polar factor for Muon-style updates.
The proposed method is mathematically motivated, with a clean minimax formulation and a useful connection between adaptive polynomial iterations and classical approximation theory.
The algorithm is GPU-friendly, simple to implement, and includes some practical finite-precision stabilizations for bfloat16 use.

The empirical section includes both controlled matrix-function experiments and end-to-end GPT-2 training runs, and the reported losses consistently favor Polar Express over the compared Muon polynomial variants.
weaknesses: The novelty is not fully convincing for a top-tier AI venue. Much of the core idea appears to be an adaptation or recombination of known minimax, Remez, Chen-Chow, and Zolotarev-style adaptive approximation ideas; the paper acknowledges closely related and concurrent work but does not clearly establish a substantial conceptual advance for AI beyond this specific Muon instantiation.

The empirical evidence is too narrow for the strength of the claims. The main deep-learning validation is limited to GPT-2 variants on FineWeb1B, with no clear multi-seed analysis, uncertainty estimates, broader architectures, downstream tasks, or scaling study beyond this setting.

The reported gains, while consistent, are modest and could plausibly depend on hyperparameter choices, the guessed lower singular-value bound, weight decay, and implementation details. The paper does not sufficiently isolate these factors.

The comparison set is incomplete. The paper focuses on Jordan, You, Newton-Schulz, Chen-Chow, and AdamW, but does not convincingly compare against stronger optimizer baselines or practical Muon variants under matched tuning and compute budgets.

Several main claims are overstated. In particular, claims such as optimality and outperforming previous methods are tied to a restricted worst-case polynomial-composition objective, not necessarily to training quality, wall-clock efficiency, or realistic gradient spectra.

Reproducibility is weaker than expected: important training details, variance, exact code availability, and implementation choices are not documented enough to make the end-to-end results easy to verify.

The paper has noticeable presentation and quality-control issues, including caption inconsistencies in the GPT-Large figure, repeated or incorrect labels, typographical errors, and some confusing notation in the appendix. These do not by themselves invalidate the work, but they reduce confidence in the care of the submission.

The significance for the broader AI community is limited. The contribution is technically plausible and potentially useful for Muon, but the paper does not demonstrate enough impact beyond a narrow optimizer subroutine to be competitive at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: Clear and meaningful contribution: the paper derives an adaptive polynomial method for polar decomposition/matrix sign computation that is directly motivated by the needs of Muon and GPU-friendly low-precision training.

Strong theoretical component: the greedy minimax construction is elegant, well positioned relative to Newton-Schulz, Padé, Chen-Chow, and Zolotarev-style methods, and is supported by convergence guarantees and detailed appendices.

Practical algorithmic presentation is unusually concrete: the paper gives coefficients, implementation-level pseudocode, bfloat16 stabilization choices, and discusses rectangular-matrix acceleration ideas.

Empirical results are convincing for the targeted application: Polar Express improves synthetic convergence, GPT-2 gradient-matrix approximation, and Muon training loss/validation loss on GPT-2 Small and Large across learning-rate sweeps.
The work is well written and bridges numerical analysis and modern deep learning optimization in a way likely to be useful to both communities.
weaknesses: The main training evaluation is still somewhat narrow: experiments are limited to GPT-2-style models on FineWeb1B, and it is unclear how robust the gains are for larger-scale pretraining, different architectures, downstream tasks, or non-language domains.

The empirical section appears to lack repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, so the statistical reliability of the reported validation-loss improvements is hard to judge, especially when gains are modest.

Some implementation choices, such as the lower-bound guess, cushioning, and safety factor, are motivated pragmatically but not fully ablated in the training setting; this leaves open how sensitive the method is in practice.

The paper has a few presentation inconsistencies and likely caption errors, particularly around Figure 7 where the reported final losses appear copied from the GPT-Small setting and conflict with the GPT-Large numbers elsewhere.

The claim of practical runtime improvement is mostly indirect for the main Muon experiments: equal degree implies similar per-iteration cost, but more detailed wall-clock breakdowns and optimizer-overhead measurements would strengthen the case.

strengths: Clear and timely contribution: the paper develops a GPU-friendly polynomial method for polar decomposition/matrix sign computation, directly motivated by Muon and low-precision deep learning workloads.

Strong technical core: the minimax composition perspective, greedy optimality result, convergence guarantee, and finite-precision stabilization give the method a principled basis beyond the heuristic coefficient searches used in recent Muon implementations.

The method is practical: it uses only matrix multiplications, has a short PyTorch implementation, supports bfloat16 use, and is a drop-in replacement for existing Newton-Schulz/Jordan/You-style iterations.

Empirical evaluation is broad and relevant: synthetic convergence tests, GPT-2 Small/Large training on 1B and 10B FineWeb tokens, weight-decay ablations, iteration-count ablations, SVD comparison, CIFAR experiments, and wall-clock/training-loss plots.

The paper is unusually transparent about when extra polar accuracy matters: the ablations showing saturation after 5-6 iterations and insensitivity to small singular directions are useful and help explain the optimizer behavior.
Presentation is generally clear, with substantial appendices for proofs, implementation details, finite-precision issues, and additional experiments.
weaknesses: The downstream gains, while consistent, are modest in several key settings, especially at 10B tokens where the gap over Jordan/You becomes small. The paper would be stronger with statistical replication or confidence intervals for the expensive GPT experiments.

The main optimality claim applies to an idealized minimax problem with fixed spectral bounds and exact arithmetic; the deployed algorithm uses stabilizing modifications and guessed lower bounds, so the practical method is not exactly the theoretically optimal object.

The choice of the lower singular-value bound is important but handled mostly by a fixed heuristic. The paper shows robustness to some misspecification, but does not provide a fully satisfactory adaptive strategy for diverse real training regimes.

Runtime benefits are somewhat indirect: the method improves loss at comparable cost to other degree-5 polynomial methods, but the ablation suggests polar computation is not a dominant runtime cost in the tested GPT setting. Thus the practical advantage is accuracy/optimization quality rather than clear throughput improvement.

The strongest AI experiments are limited to GPT-2-scale language models and CIFAR-scale vision models. Evidence on larger modern transformer training, instruction/fine-tuning regimes, or non-Muon optimizer variants would strengthen the impact claim.

Some comparisons to classical rational/QR/SVD-based polar methods are mostly qualitative or relegated to discussion; although this is reasonable for GPU/deep-learning constraints, more empirical runtime/accuracy context would help readers outside the Muon niche.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: fast GPU-friendly polar/sign computations inside Muon-style optimizers for deep learning.

The core formulation is clean: viewing iterative polar-factor methods as compositions of low-degree odd polynomials gives a useful lens, and the greedy minimax optimality result is mathematically appealing within the stated class.
The proposed implementation is simple, dependency-light, and plausibly useful in practice; the inclusion of finite-precision considerations for bfloat16 is valuable.
The experiments include both synthetic convergence tests and GPT-2 training runs, with ablations over iteration count, weight decay, and training-token budget.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat limited. The method is closely related to prior adaptive polynomial/sign iterations, especially Chen and Chow and Lee et al.; the main theoretical contribution is an optimality statement under a restrictive polynomial-composition class rather than a broadly new algorithmic paradigm.

The central practical claims are stronger than the evidence. Most compelling optimizer results are on GPT-2/FineWeb with Muon, and gains over Jordan/You shrink substantially in the 10B-token setting. The paper does not establish that the method matters across modern architectures, larger-scale LLM settings, or diverse optimizer configurations.

The empirical evaluation lacks important rigor for a top-tier venue: limited reporting of random seeds/variance for language-model experiments, no statistical testing, incomplete wall-clock/memory profiling, and limited comparison to all relevant adaptive polynomial methods, including very recent/concurrent alternatives.

The advertised optimality does not fully transfer to the deployed algorithm. The practical implementation uses cushioning, safety scaling, hard-coded lower-bound assumptions, and bfloat16 modifications that break or weaken the exact minimax story, but the gap between theorem and implementation is not quantified sufficiently.

The choice of lower singular-value bound is heuristic and potentially fragile. The paper argues that bad guesses only delay convergence, yet the experiments show sensitivity, and it is unclear how robust the default is across real training regimes, layers, precisions, and non-LLM applications.

The image-classification results in the appendix weaken the broader significance: Muon variants perform similarly there, suggesting the method's benefit may be narrow to particular language-model/Muon settings.

Reproducibility is only partially convincing from the manuscript: code is said to be in supplementary material, but the main paper relies on hard-coded coefficients and does not provide enough detail to independently reproduce all large-scale training results from the text alone.

Presentation occasionally overclaims, e.g. language such as 'state-of-the-art' and 'converge as rapidly as possible' should be more carefully scoped to the precise approximation class, assumptions, and modified finite-precision algorithm.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important bottleneck in Muon-style optimization: fast GPU-friendly approximation of the polar factor using only matrix multiplications.

The main technical contribution is clear and elegant: the adaptive polynomial updates are formulated as minimax approximations, with a greedy optimality result and super-exponential convergence guarantees. This gives a principled basis for coefficient choices that were previously heuristic.

The method is simple to implement and deploy. The paper provides concise PyTorch-style implementation details, offline coefficient computation, and finite-precision modifications for bfloat16, which are important for the intended deep learning use case.

The empirical evaluation is strong for a methods paper of this type: synthetic convergence studies, GPT-2 Small/Large training on 1B tokens, longer 10B-token runs, weight-decay ablations, iteration-count ablations, comparisons to Jordan/You/Newton-Schulz and AdamW where relevant, plus additional CIFAR/ResNet/ViT experiments.

The results support the central claims: Polar Express consistently gives better polar approximation quality and usually improves Muon training loss/validation loss at equal per-iteration polynomial degree. The exact-SVD ablation usefully clarifies that coarse-but-targeted approximations are sufficient for Muon.
The paper is well positioned relative to numerical linear algebra and recent Muon practice, and it makes a convincing bridge between approximation theory and modern optimizer engineering.
weaknesses: The practical training gains, while consistent, are often modest. On the 10B-token GPT-2-Large run the improvement over You/Jordan is small, and on CIFAR/ViT the advantage is weak or absent. This somewhat limits the demonstrated impact outside the main GPT/Muon setting.

The LLM experiments appear to use limited or no random-seed replication, so it is hard to assess variance and statistical significance of the reported validation-loss improvements. Given the small margins in several settings, stronger uncertainty estimates would improve confidence.

The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior adaptive Newton-Schulz/sign-function work, especially Chen & Chow and classical minimax/Remez methods. The paper’s contribution is mainly adapting and packaging these ideas for Muon with a clean optimality argument rather than inventing a fundamentally new numerical paradigm.

The method depends on a chosen lower singular-value bound and finite-precision stabilizations that are partly heuristic, such as the safety factor and cushioning thresholds. The paper studies sensitivity, but a more systematic analysis of these engineering choices would strengthen the claims.

The main application evidence is concentrated on GPT-2-scale language models and Muon. It remains unclear whether the approach materially improves larger frontier-scale training, non-transformer domains, or optimizers beyond Muon.

Some reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript text as extracted, notably the supplementary source-code location appears blank, and exact seed counts/hardware/runtime accounting could be clearer. There are also minor presentation issues and apparent typos in appendix algorithms.
